questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The thrust a masonry arch contains
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a masonry arch is described as containing a thrust
questions.stem: The client asks you to explain in writing why a semicircular masonry arch over a temple doorway is described as containing a thrust rather than simply carrying weight.

answer.exemplar: An arch does not carry its load straight down to the ground. The wedge-shaped blocks press on one another and turn the weight into a line of compression that runs around the curve, but that line ends by pushing sideways into the two abutments. That sideways push is the thrust, and it is the reason an arch needs heavy, stiff supports rather than a simple wall below.

questions.explanation: Thrust is the sideways component of the load that the arch delivers into its supports. A freestanding arch has nowhere to send it unless the abutments supply the mass.
questions.hint: Name the sideways push the arch sends into its supports.

questions.topic: The thrust a masonry arch contains

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A free arch span with no buttress behind it
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a free arch needs haunch weight or a tie
questions.stem: Write a note for the client explaining why an arch left free with no buttress behind it is described as the most demanding form of the arch, and what a designer does about it.

answer.exemplar: A free arch has no massive support behind it, so the sideways thrust it generates at the springing has nothing to absorb it. The designer answers by thickening the haunches so their own weight pulls the curve back into equilibrium, or by tying the two supports together with a concealed tie, or by proposing a pointed profile whose thrust is smaller for the same span.

questions.explanation: The weight of the haunches and any tie must balance the thrust exactly. Without that balance the springing feet spread and the arch hinges, dropping the crown.
questions.hint: Explain how the sideways push is held in balance.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The load path of a barrel vault
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a barrel vault delivers its load to the side walls
questions.stem: Explain to a client why a barrel vault is described as carrying its load along a curve to the side walls rather than straight down to the ground.

answer.exemplar: A barrel vault is one continuous arch extended along a straight axis, so the weight of the vaulting and the roof above it is resolved into a line of compression that runs around the curve. That line ends by pushing outward into the two parallel walls that spring the vault, and those walls must then carry the push down into their own foundations rather than passing the weight straight to the ground.

questions.explanation: Because the vault behaves as a continuous arch, its load is resolved sideways rather than vertically. The side walls therefore do the structural work of the arches they carry.
questions.hint: Say which walls receive the load and what they must do.

questions.stem: Explain to a colleague why the arch over a temple doorway is described as containing its load, and what the term thrust adds to that description.

answer.exemplar: Containing the load means the arch does not let the weight fall straight to the ground as a lintel would. The voussoirs form a wedge that transfers the weight around the curve and finally delivers it to the two abutments. questions.explanation: The diagonal of a 12.0 metre square is 12.0 x 1.4142 = 16.97 metres. The circle spans 12.0 metres, so it falls 16.97 - 12.0 = 4.97 metres short of the corner, and that gap is what the pendentives fill.
questions.hint: Compare the diagonal with the width of the bay.

questions.topic: The temple plan as a diagram of belief
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a temple plan states a claim about belief
questions.stem: Write a short paragraph for the donor explaining how a temple plan can be read as a statement about belief rather than as a neutral arrangement of rooms.

answer.exemplar: A neutral plan would only record where rooms sit. A diagram of belief claims that the order of those rooms matters, and it does so through the body of the visitor. questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The load path of a barrel vault
questions.learningObjective: Trace the full load path from barrel vault to foundations
questions.stem: Explain to a client how the load of a barrel vault reaches the ground, naming every part of the path in order.

answer.exemplar: The weight of the vaulting and the roof above it is gathered by the curve of the barrel and carried along that curve to the two springing walls. The walls then pass the load down through their own thickness into the foundations beneath, which spread it into the ground. The whole path is a chain of compression, and any weak link in it, the vault, the wall, or the footing, becomes the failure point.

questions.explanation: The path runs from the vaulting along the curve, into the springing walls, and down into the foundations. Each stage of that chain must be strong enough for the stage before it.
questions.hint: Name the parts the load passes through, in order.

questions.topic: Squinches and pendentives as a geometric transition
questions.learningObjective: Explain how squinches and pendentives each close a domed square bay
questions.stem: Explain in writing how a squinch and a pendentive each solve the problem of carrying a round dome over a square bay.

answer.exemplar: A dome is round at its base, but the room below is square, so the corners of the square have to be closed off before the circle can begin. A squinch does this with a small arch built across each corner, so that the arch itself carries the load inward to the circle. A pendentive does it with a curved triangular surface of masonry that rises from the corner, thickens toward the base, and meets the others to form the circle.

questions.explanation: Both devices close the four corners of the square so the dome can spring from a circle. One uses an arch, the other a continuous curved surface.
questions.hint: Both solve the same corner problem in different ways.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a column grid is read as a statement about space
questions.stem: Explain to a colleague why the column grid of a hypostyle hall is read as a statement about the space rather than a set of supports.

answer.exemplar: The columns are identical, evenly spaced, and run without interruption across the whole hall, so no single column is more important than any other. The hall is thereby presented as one continuous field rather than as a set of privileged bays, and that field is what carries the sacred weight.

questions.explanation: A uniform, repeated grid makes the space itself the object of attention. The supports are deliberately undifferentiated so that the hall can be read as a single field.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The load path of a barrel vault
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a vault-carrying wall must be thicker than an ordinary wall
questions.stem: Explain to a client what a barrel vault does to the walls that carry it, and why the wall section must be thicker than an ordinary wall of the same height.

answer.exemplar: A barrel vault pushes outward as well as down, so the wall that springs it has to take a sideways thrust from the vault as well as its own weight. A plain wall is sized only for the load above it and for its own stability, but a vault-carrying wall must also be stiff and massive enough to hold that thrust without moving. Thickening the section is the cheapest way to add the weight and breadth needed to resist the push.

questions.explanation: The vault delivers a horizontal component of load into the wall. A thicker section supplies the mass and stiffness needed to resist that push.
questions.hint: Say what extra force the wall must take from the vault.
